newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan passes long-delayed Futures Trading Law.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan passes long-delayed Futures Trading Law.

text.p: Taiwan's parliament on Tuesday adopted a long-delayed Futures Trading Law, clearing the only obstacle to establishment of the island's first futures exchange, possibly within six months.
"We passed the Futures Trading Law and we want to see the finance ministry authorise establishment of an exchange house within six months," legislator Lin Chung-cheng told Reuters by telephone.
Officials had said protracted parliamentary bickering over the draft law during 1996 and into 1997 had forced authorities to push back the planned exchange's launch date to 1998 at the earliest.

Lee Chi-hsien, deputy director of the futures department of the watchdog Securities and Exchange Commission, hailed word of the law's passage, but cautioned that opening by October 1997 would require fast organisational work.
"The exchange could open as early as October, but we need much more detailled regulation to ensure smooth operation and prevent potential financial irregularities," Lee said.
Lee said that once an exchange is established, the first contracts to be traded would be futures linked to the benchmark TAIEX index managed by the island's main Taiwan Stock Exchange.

Such contracts would offer the first domestic alternative to unauthorised offshore Taiwan stock index futures launched on January 9 by the Chicago Mercantile Exchange and the Singapore International Monetary Exchange, or SIMEX.

Analysts say pressure from the offshore rivals helped prompt lawmakers to resolve deep differences over three versions of the draft law to prevent local investors from turning to the CME and SIMEX contracts for a stock market hedge.

Once index futures are launched, the exchange would begin rolling out commodity-related contracts linked to Taiwan's voracious appetite for soybeans, corn and wheat, Lee said. Metals contracts were unlikely in the early stages, he said.
The central bank would have final say over all financial futures offered by the Taiwan exchange, Lee added.

Taiwan futures houses already are allowed to offer a wide range of major overseas futures contracts, but to date only the CME and SIMEX futures contracts were linked directly to Taiwan's own economy. San Francisco's Pacific Stock Exchange has offered Taiwan stock-index options since January 9.
Despite tremendous pressure at the time of the CME and SIMEX launches, Taiwan still forbids Taiwan investors to trade the offshore contracts through Taiwan futures houses.
Many investors are believed to be skirting the ban by placing orders through offshore brokers, a practice that has compounded pressure on Taiwan to offer a domestic alternative.
The central bank hinted on Saturday that it might be willing to lift the ban, saying it would "cautiously support" allowing Taiwan investors to trade the CME, SIMEX and Pacific contracts.
No final decision had been taken, officials said.
Analysts have cautioned that even if Taipei lifted the ban, investors would not have direct access to the offshore contracts before midyear due to a mandatory six-month government review.
Taiwan's government traditionally has been leery of futures, regarding them as a high-risk financial instrument all but indistinguishable from gambling.
